lessons.intro: What is the difference between the Internet and the World Wide Web?
lessons.summary: In the 1960s governments in some advanced countries made efforts to get scientists to invent a system to share information through computers, and the researchers introduced a new and cheap communication system. The Internet is an electronic communications network that connects computer networks around the world; it depends on codes called internet protocols. The World Wide Web is an information system that enables content sharing over the Internet in user-friendly ways. It was invented by Tim Berners-Lee in late 1989, with the first web server, the first web browser and HTML. HTML was published in 1991 and the browser source code released in 1993; Mosaic (later Netscape Navigator) sparked the Internet boom of the 1990s. Websites for the public appeared in 1993–94, and social media, common in the 2010s, made the Web ubiquitous in everyday life.
points: Internet = network of networks (protocols).
Web = information system working over the Internet.
Tim Berners-Lee, 1989: server, browser, HTML.
Have + somebody + base verb; get + somebody + to-infinitive.

objectives: Discuss ideas: ask for and give opinions.

lessons.intro: What do you do to improve your English outside the classroom?
lessons.summary: Teachers of English as a foreign language must develop four skills: listening, speaking, reading and writing, with activities adapted to the students’ level. Alioun, a 7th year English teacher, says that learning to write and speak fluently does not come easily and needs continuous efforts. Brahim thinks a 7th year student has no extra time; Ramata disagrees: they can attend evening classes in an English centre twice a week. Sidina advises starting a vocabulary book and noting every new word with its synonyms and phrases. The teacher adds: read a broad range of English newspapers (broadsheets, magazines, tabloids) to keep up-to-date, expand your vocabulary and learn spelling and context.

lessons.title: Unit 3: Protecting the environment
objectives: Describe sequences of actions with sequencers.
Use imperatives and the passive voice.

lessons.intro: What small actions can you do every day to protect the planet?
lessons.summary: The environment faces pollution, deforestation and climate change, but small actions by individuals lead to big improvements. First, reduce waste: avoid too much packaging, use reusable bags, bottles and containers. Next, recycle plastics, glass and paper, and donate old clothes and furniture. Then, turn off lights and appliances when not in use and use energy-efficient bulbs. After that, protect water: turn off taps while brushing your teeth and fix leaks immediately, because clean water is limited. Later, plant trees: they absorb carbon dioxide and produce oxygen. Finally, join local groups and sign petitions so that governments pass laws that reduce pollution. Protecting the environment starts with you.
points: Steps: reduce, recycle, save energy, protect water, plant trees, join groups.
Sequencers: first, next, then, after that, later, finally.
Imperatives give instructions: Turn off the lights.
Passive: be + past participle: Waste is reduced.
Trees absorb CO₂ and produce oxygen.

Salem says Mahmoud should know more since he wants to be a mining engineer, and Mahmoud says it is his best trip.

lessons.summary: Baba was daydreaming: he hopes to visit Thiam’s hometown, Kaédi, next year. Thiam wishes Baba could come with him now. lessons.intro: What qualities do you look for in a friend?
lessons.summary: An ideal friend is someone the writer has always dreamed of having. He wants his friend to be honest and trustworthy, someone he can rely on in any situation, who supports him during tough times. He would like his friend to share similar interests: sports, reading, travelling. Another quality is kindness: a friend who listens when he is upset and gives advice, encourages him to chase his dreams and motivates him to do his best. In short, his ideal friend would be loyal, caring and fun to be with.

lessons.intro: Do you prefer studying alone or in a group? Why?
lessons.summary: Ousman and Khady discuss their study preferences before the history exam. Ousman prefers studying in the morning when he is fresh; Khady likes studying in the evening when it is quiet. Khady enjoys group study because talking about the material helps her, while Ousman prefers studying alone because groups distract him. Khady likes flashcards; Ousman prefers writing summaries and watching videos for tricky topics. Khady prefers total silence, so she studies at the library, but Ousman would rather study at home because it is more comfortable.

objectives: Express agreement, partial agreement and disagreement.

lessons.intro: Should violent sports like boxing be banned?
lessons.summary: Sport has become very common: jogging, swimming, friendly matches, even marathons and triathlons. Doing exercise is good news, as studies show it improves our quality of life and prolongs life expectancy. Some sports such as football, tennis, volleyball and swimming are useful and less dangerous. The writer believes that violent sports such as rugby, boxing and wrestling should be prohibited: boxing is the most grueling sport, American football the most violent, and wrestling causes bruises, broken bones and even brain damage. Gymnastics is not violent but may be dangerous. Agreeing or disagreeing depends on people’s cultural, physical and social background.

lessons.intro: What do you need to prepare for a job interview?
lessons.summary: Ms Roberts has a job interview. All candidates are required to bring a printed CV; she prepared it beforehand. As a team leader she must handle group dynamics; she managed a team of five and organized weekly check-ins. She will be required to attend interdepartmental meetings and may work some weekends at peak times; she is flexible. She manages her time by setting priorities and breaking tasks into steps. The company encourages sustainability (less paper, recycling), and she agrees we ought to contribute. New employees must complete a one-week onboarding programme and review the company handbook.

lessons.title: Unit 8 – Lesson 3: A leap into the unknown
match: Unit 8 – Lesson 3: A leap into the unknown
objectives: Express certainty and uncertainty.
Use must, have to, definitely, might, may, could, probably.
Understand a short story.
lessons.intro: How do you feel before an important decision?
lessons.summary: Amina stands at the airport gate, about to board a plane to a country she has never visited. She tries to convince herself it is the right decision, but uncertainty lingers. Her mother has no doubt she will succeed; her father hesitates: it might not be as easy as she thinks. Amina replied that she is certain this is what she wants. Alone in the terminal, doubt creeps in: what if she doesn’t fit in or struggles with the language? She reminds herself that things may be difficult at first, but she will adapt. At the final boarding call she whispers, « I must trust myself », and steps forward.
points: Amina leaves for an unknown country.
Mother: certainty; father: doubt.
Certainty: must, have to, definitely, I’m certain.
Uncertainty: might, may, could, probably, possibly.
Final decision: she trusts herself.
